subject: Markov properties related to SMC/particle sampling?

messages.author: 6fee017125c7bf75
messages.subject: Markov properties related to SMC/particle sampling?
parts:
Hi all,

I’ve got a combo of a theoretical/coding question and I’m hoping one you may have some insights. 

Say we have a state-space model with Y_t vector of data at time t and X_t latent unobserved states (below example from Michaud paper) with some function f and g.

Y_t ~ g(y_t | x_t, theta)
X_t ~ f(x_t | x_t-1, theta)

I know that f() is specifying the Markov properties of the state-space model (correct me if I’m wrong).

The question I have is that if we use something like SMC or a particle filter does the sampler actually use x_t-1 to estimate the x_t latents states? When I look at the algorithms this does not seem to be the case because the particle filter is estimating the marginal likelihood based on a proposal for theta (for example) and then you can draw the latent states after completing y_1:T (at least this is what I think).I just want to be sure that I know what it’s doing under the hood.

This is related to my previous question because I'm trying to use the accepted latent state (location in my case) to sample for the location of a covariate to use in my model. I don't want it to use x_t-1 to sample the location, I want it to use x_t.

Hopefully this questions makes sense.

Best,
Rowenna

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Markov properties related to SMC/particle sampling?
parts:
Hi Rowenna,

Thanks for the question.  This sounds like an interesting application.

The particle filters work by simulating many states at each time step.  The states are weighted and/or resampled at each step.  The basic idea of the theory behind using this in PMCMC is that if the Monte Carlo likelihood approximation is unbiased, it can be used in Metropolis-Hastings updates.

I believe that if the latent states are in the monitors (which they will likely not be by default), they will be drawn from particle filter results and put in the model so they can be recorded in the MCMC output.  I guess it would then be the case that other parameters could be updated conditional on the states.  I'm not sure we've tested that case, so please do stay in touch if you try it.  I think the system was written with the idea that all top-level parameters would be sampled by PMCMC (RW_PF) samplers.

I am not sure I follow your last sentence.  Can you explain more if this hasn't addressed your question?

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: Markov properties related to SMC/particle sampling?
parts:
This is great Perry - thanks.

The last part of my question is related to how the model is written in nimble. 

If we still have some observation model Y_t ~ g(y_t | x_t, theta)

and our process model is 

X_t ~ exp(beta_0 + beta_1*covar_1)

where covar_1 is a covariate sampled at the location of x_t.

To write this in nimble is where I start to get more hung up. 

We can't write

x[t] ~ exp(beta0 + beta1*covar1[x[t]]) because, I believe, that nimble sees that as cyclic, which it is. 

x[t] ~ exp(beta0 + beta1*covar1[x[t-1]]) isn't cyclic but I can't figure out if this will influence the sampler or just indicate the markov properties. 

Hopefully this explains the last part of my question better.

Cheers,
Rowenna

messages.subject: Re: Markov properties related to SMC/particle sampling?
parts:
Hi Rowenna,

Thanks for the extra explanation.  So x[t] is indexed by time, and it sounds like you are referring to it as being associated with space?  Can you explain more what that means?  That sounds a little unusual, or is this an animal movement model?

Since the x[t]s are not integer-valued, I'm not getting the idea of using them as indices, as in covar1[x[t-1]].

If covar1 does not need to be calculated from the value of x[t-1], you can use something like 
x[t] ~ exp(beta0 + beta1*covar1[t-1])
where you provide covar1[t-1], with indices aligned however you need them (offset by one in time, or not, or indexed simply by t if you want).

If covar1 is stochastically related to x[t-1], I think you can make this work by increasing the number of latent states, but I'm not getting what you're trying to do.

If x[t] is a continuous location and you have a discretized grid of locations corresponding to covar1 values, I think you could use something like this:

covar1_index[t-1] <- calculate_grid_index(x[t-1])
x[t] ~ exp(beta0 + beta1*covar1[ covar1_index[t-1] ])

where you would write calculate_grid_index as a nimbleFunction or nimbleRcall or simply model code that converts a continuous location x to an integer index in a grid indexing scheme you would need to set up.  Since you've shown x as one dimensional, I'm not sure of your setup.

That is a bit of a guess but is a kind of application I've seen.

Can you please clarify more if I'm still not getting it.

-Perry

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Markov properties related to SMC/particle sampling?
parts:
In case anyone was interested in this thread, I'm posting a follow-up on the list.  Rowenna and I continued discussion off-list (accidentally!).  This is a case of an animal movement model where a spatially indexed covariate helps predict where animals will move.  Hence one can set up a spatial grid and use a categorical distribution (dcat) of which grid cell an animal will move to, with the probabilities calculated using the covariate conditional on current location, or one could write a custom distribution to accomplish this.  (A related point is that MCMC sampling with latent states that follow dcat with many categories can be slow because the default sampler will try every category on every iteration, although in this case PMCMC was of interest).

-Perry
